title: Model versioning
story:
A model version is a dependency, and it is the only dependency in your system that can change what your software does without anyone changing your software. That single property is what makes this worth a lesson of its own, because every habit you have for managing dependencies assumes that nothing moves unless you move it.

Start by writing down what a version actually consists of here, because it is not one thing. The weights, obviously. But also the decoding settings — how much randomness, how long the output may be, what stops it — because two identical models with different settings are two different systems from the user's point of view. The prompt that ships alongside them. The tokeniser. Anything in the serving stack that changes how the output is produced. If you record only the model name, you have recorded the smallest part of it, and you will eventually be unable to explain a change nobody made.

Pin what you can, and know what you cannot. A hosted model behind a general name will move underneath you, on a schedule you do not control, and when that happens the symptom is not an error but a shift in behaviour that arrives without a deploy. That is the situation to design for: something in your product changed and your change log is empty. Pin to a specific version where the provider offers one, record on every request which version answered it, and treat a version change as a deploy even though you did not make it.

The corollary is that deprecation is an operational event with a deadline. A version you depend on will eventually be withdrawn, usually with less notice than you would like, and the work to migrate is not a configuration change — it is running your case set against the new version, finding what shifted, adjusting prompts that were tuned to the old one, and deciding whether the difference is acceptable. That takes real time, so the deprecation notice needs to become a scheduled piece of work rather than a message somebody saw in an email.

When you do move, move the way you would with any other risky dependency. Run the new version beside the old on real or replayed traffic, compare against the case set, look at the disagreements rather than the aggregate — the aggregate can stay flat while a category of question quietly gets worse — and keep the route back until you are sure. The ability to return to the previous version is the entire safety mechanism, and it is usually lost by accident, because a prompt was edited to suit the new version and no longer works with the old.

One more habit worth adopting, and it costs almost nothing. Keep the outputs your system produced for your case set at each version, not just the scores. Scores tell you something changed; the stored outputs tell you what. When somebody asks why the answers feel different this month, a side-by-side of the same twenty questions across two versions answers it in minutes, and without that you are reasoning about a system you can no longer observe in its previous state.

problem.invariant: The output is determined by the whole configuration, so a version is the weights together with the settings and the prompt that shipped with them, not the model name alone.
problem.breaks: A hosted version moves on a schedule you do not control and the symptom is behaviour rather than an error, so nothing in your normal change process will flag it.

problem.practice: Find out, for your own system, exactly which model version answered a request from last month — not the family name, the version. If you cannot, that is the gap, and fixing it is one field added to a log line. Then store the case-set outputs alongside it, so the next comparison takes minutes rather than an argument.

beats.broke: A model can change what your product does with no change to your code, and the normal dependency habits assume nothing moves unless you move it.
beats.fix: Record the whole configuration per request, pin where possible, treat a provider's change as an unplanned deploy, and keep case-set outputs at each version.
beats.cost: Every migration is scheduled work — run the set, inspect disagreements, re-tune prompts — and the route back has to be protected deliberately.

interview.q: What makes a model version different from any other dependency, and what has to be recorded?
interview.trap: Recording the model family name only. The output depends on the decoding settings and the shipped prompt too, so the name alone cannot explain a behaviour change.
interview.answer:
It can change what the software does without anyone changing the software, which breaks the assumption behind every dependency habit — that nothing moves unless you move it.

What I record is the whole configuration: weights, decoding settings such as randomness, maximum length and stop conditions, the prompt that ships with them, the tokeniser, and anything in the serving stack that shapes output. Two identical models with different settings are two different systems to a user, so the model name alone is the smallest part of it.

Then I pin where a specific version exists, record on every request which version answered, and treat a provider-side change as a deploy I did not make — because the symptom is a behaviour shift with an empty change log rather than an error.

Deprecation becomes scheduled work with a deadline, since migrating means running the case set, finding what shifted, re-tuning prompts fitted to the old version and judging whether the difference is acceptable.

Moving is done like any risky dependency: new beside old on real or replayed traffic, comparing disagreements rather than the aggregate, because the aggregate can stay flat while one category quietly degrades — and protecting the route back, which is usually lost when a prompt is edited to suit the new version.

And I store the outputs for the case set at each version, not only the scores, because scores say something changed and the outputs say what.
